units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: World Models and Dreamer

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Learn to act entirely inside imagined experience.

sections.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Section one, Learning to walk from camera frames

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 1. The loop runs in three panels. The first panel learns how the world works from real camera frames. The second imagines ahead in a short summary of each frame and learns to act there. The third acts in the real environment and stores what happened. So the loop keeps turning: real play teaches the model, the model supplies fresh practice, and the walker gets better each round.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Each round of real play teaches the model, and the model supplies fresh practice, so each new real episode makes the walker better.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: The running example is a walker, a two-legged robot that must learn to walk forward, seen only through a camera. The camera follows the walker from the side as it moves.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 2. The walker is shown as its camera sees it, mid-stride, one leg forward and the other pushing off. The camera shows only this picture, never the joints, so the learner must work out where the body is from the picture alone.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: The camera shows only this picture, never the joints, so the learner must work out where the body is.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: A robot that learns from camera images by trial and error needs a huge amount of real practice, and real practice is slow and costly.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Here the agent is the program that drives the walker's joints, turning each camera frame into motor commands. In each frame the walker is in a state, its situation right now; the agent picks a move, one choice it can make in that state, and the world hands back a reward, a number, good or bad, after each move.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: DeepMind Control is a set of simulated robot tasks, such as this walker. An observation is what the agent senses at one moment, here the camera frame.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: The walker is paid for moving forward while staying upright. A real step is one move made in the real environment, with the reward and the next state it brings. On the walker each real step runs the simulated robot forward and renders a new camera frame, so real steps are the expensive part.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Each move is a set of torques, one for each joint, and there is no short list of moves to try. A torque is a turning force a motor applies at a joint. A continuous action is a real number, or a list of them, that can take any value in a range, like a torque, instead of one choice from a list.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: 1.1 World Models played games inside its own guess

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: The world model

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Picture the walker seen only through its camera: a world model is the learner's guess of how the world works, built from frames.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Squeeze each frame into a hidden state, a short list of numbers, guess how it changes after each torque, predict the reward, and rebuild the frame.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: When the guess is good, the walker practises inside the guess instead of paying for real steps.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Dreamer grew from World Models, which learned a guess of two games and played one of them entirely inside that guess. Dreamer keeps that idea and fixes two gaps: training in stages, and a controller kept tiny by learning without gradients.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Latent means hidden: learned by the network rather than observed directly.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: CarRacing is a top-down driving game, and VizDoom Take Cover is a first-person game where the player must dodge fireballs. A recurrent network is a network that carries a memory from one step to the next.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: World Models squeezed each frame into a short list of numbers, and used a recurrent network to learn how those numbers change. On top sat a controller, a tiny network that picks the moves from those numbers and the memory's summary of the past. The model's temperature sets how much randomness it adds when it imagines: hotter means more random.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: In VizDoom the controller trained only inside the imagined game, and a higher temperature made tricks that only work there harder to find.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: On CarRacing the full model, with vision and memory, scored 906 ± 21 over 100 trials, past 900, the score the task sets as solved, after learning from 10,000 runs of random play; the vision-only version, which keeps no memory from one frame to the next, scored only 632 ± 251. In Take Cover a temperature of 0.1 scored 2086 inside the imagined game but only 193 for real, while 1.15 scored 1092 for real.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: 1.2 World Models trained in stages and kept its controller tiny

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: World Models trained the frame-squeezing part and the predicting part first, from random play, and only then the controller on top. Dreamer keeps training its model on new real experience while its behaviour learns.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: World Models trained its controller by trial and error with CMA-ES, which tries many weight settings and keeps and recombines the best. That ignores the gradients the model could offer, how the reward would change for a slightly different torque, so the controller had to stay tiny. Dreamer learns its behaviour by gradients through the model, so its networks can be large.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: Dreamer's imagined rollouts start from real moments the walker has lived. One imagined step is one move tried inside the model; an imagined rollout is a run of them, each starting where the last one ended.

units.section: 1 Learning to walk from camera frames
units.spoken: The walker needs a rule for choosing a move in each state. A policy is that rule; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. Model exploitation means the policy finds actions where the learned model is wrong and scores well only in imagination. World Models' controller found moves that made the imagined game's fireballs vanish, a trick that failed in the real game. Dreamer also learns its behaviour inside a model, so the walker faces the same risk.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Section two, The walker practises without moving

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Learning in imagination

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Picture the walker practising without moving: the actor that picks the torques and the critic that scores states train only on rollouts the world model makes up.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Start from a real hidden state, step the model forward without new frames, and let the actor pick torques, each step earning its reward.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: When a round lands, one real step buys many practice steps, and the actor never sees a real frame. Each real episode buys 100 training steps on batches of 50 stored sequences, each a run of frames, torques and rewards from real play.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 3. One real hidden state starts the rollout. From that one state the actor picks torques and the critic scores states, and every imagined step grows from the start the walker has actually lived.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Every imagined step grows from that one hidden state, so the actor and critic learn from a start the walker has actually lived.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Picture the walker mid-stride. A fall early on loses all the return it would have earned by walking on: one run from the start until it ends is an episode , and the return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less .

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: From any pose, the walker still has return to earn: a state's value is that expected return. A critic is a second network that guesses each state's value, the return expected from it. The critic lets Dreamer value what lies past the end of a short imagined rollout.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Dreamer's actor picks the torques; for amounts like these it gives a range of likely torques instead of a chance per move.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Latent dynamics are the world model's rules for how the hidden state changes from one step to the next. Both learn from the same imagined rollouts.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: The real world gives no gradient, but the learned model is a network, so the actor learns how a small change in its torques changes later imagined rewards.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Exploration noise is a small random nudge added to the actor's actions while it learns, so the agent tries moves it is not sure about. The actor plays real episodes with this noise added to its torques.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: 2.1 Short imagined rollouts with a critic at the end

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Dreamer imagines only a short way ahead from each real moment. That length, the planning horizon, also called the imagination horizon, is how many steps each imagined rollout runs before a critic values the rest. Here the horizon H counts imagined steps, while the H on the Soft Actor-Critic page means entropy, how undecided the policy is. A short horizon is safe but short-sighted.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: Each imagined step starts from the last imagined state, so a small model error grows the further ahead the agent imagines. So the longer Dreamer imagines, the less it can trust the end, where the critic takes over.

units.section: 2 Imagined rollouts replace a simulator
units.spoken: PlaNet is a planner that plans inside a learned model: before every real step it tries many sequences of actions inside the model and plays the first move of the best one, then plans again from scratch. It never needs a critic but pays for a fresh plan at every step. Reach for it when a fresh plan at every step is affordable and no actor needs training. An actor trained on imagined rewards alone, without a critic, sees reward only inside the horizon, as PlaNet does. Dreamer imagines these short rollouts from many stored real moments at once.

sections.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Section three, Three networks learn inside imagination

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: 3.1 Frames become hidden states

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The world model is a recurrent state space model, an RSSM: its hidden state has two parts, a deterministic memory that carries the past forward and a random state drawn fresh at each step.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. This is the world model in five lines: guess the hidden state with the frame, guess it without the frame, predict the reward, rebuild the frame, and carry the memory forward.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Equation 1. The world model. The walker is seen only through a camera, so the learner never sees its joints directly and must work from frames.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The first line. p sub omega is the guess that uses the frame. s hat sub t is the hidden state it gives chances over. s hat sub t minus 1 is the last hidden state. a sub t minus 1 is the last torques. o sub t is the walker's camera frame. So the guess that uses the frame gives chances over the hidden state, given the last state, the last torques and the frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The frame pins down the hidden state behind the pose.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. p sub omega is the guess that uses the frame, the chances over the hidden state, with the small omega under it the weights. s hat sub t is the hidden state the guess gives chances over, random because the model is unsure and keeps several possible states, each with its chance. The bar reads as given. The brackets hold what the guess takes in: s hat sub t minus 1 , the last hidden state, a sub t minus 1 , the last torques, and o sub t , the walker's camera frame. p sub omega of s hat sub t given s hat sub t minus 1 , a sub t minus 1 and o sub t is the guess that uses the frame. The small t under each symbol marks the real step. The guess that works without the frame, q sub omega of s hat sub t given s hat sub t minus 1 and a sub t minus 1 , guesses the same state without the frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. Picture the walker mid-stride, one leg forward and the other pushing off: the frame shows that pose, and the guess that uses the frame pins down the hidden state behind it.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The second line. q sub omega is the guess that works without the frame. s hat sub t is the next hidden state it gives chances over. s hat sub t minus 1 is the last hidden state. a sub t minus 1 is the last torques. So the guess that works without the frame predicts the next hidden state from the last state and the last torques alone.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. Without the frame, the next hidden state is guessed from the last state and the last torques alone.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. q sub omega is the guess that works without the frame, the chances over the next hidden state, with the small omega under it the model's weights. s hat sub t is the next hidden state the guess gives chances over. The bar reads as given. The brackets hold what the guess takes in: s hat sub t minus 1 , the last hidden state, and a sub t minus 1 , the last torques, and nothing else, no frame. q sub omega of s hat sub t given s hat sub t minus 1 and a sub t minus 1 is the guess that works without the frame. This is the transition line, the latent dynamics: how the hidden state changes from one step to the next. Imagination uses only this line and the reward line.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. Start from the hidden state behind the mid-stride pose: from that state and the last torques, the guess that works without the frame predicts the next hidden state without any new frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The third line. q sub omega is the guess that predicts from the hidden state alone. r sub t is the reward it gives chances over. s hat sub t is the hidden state. So the reward guess says what arriving at a hidden state is worth.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The reward guess says what arriving at a hidden state is worth.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. q sub omega is the guess that predicts from the hidden state alone, with the small omega under it the model's weights. r sub t is the reward the guess gives chances over: the points the walker earned by arriving there. The bar reads as given. The brackets hold the one input, s hat sub t , the hidden state. q sub omega of r sub t given s hat sub t is the reward guess. That same guess, q sub omega of o sub t given s hat sub t , also rebuilds the frame from the hidden state.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. With the walker upright after a step: the reward guess predicts the points for staying upright.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The fourth line. q sub omega is the guess that predicts from the hidden state alone. o sub t is the frame it gives chances over. s hat sub t is the hidden state. So the guess that rebuilds the frame redraws what the camera should show.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. Rebuilding the frame is what teaches the hidden state to carry what the camera shows.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. q sub omega is the guess that predicts from the hidden state alone, with the small omega under it the model's weights. o sub t is the frame the guess gives chances over: what the walker's camera would show if the hidden state were right. The bar reads as given. The brackets hold the one input, s hat sub t , the hidden state. q sub omega of o sub t given s hat sub t is the guess that rebuilds the frame. Only the guess that uses the frame sees it; every other guess predicts from the hidden state alone. The whole equation is the model: see the frame, guess ahead without it, predict the reward, and rebuild the frame to learn from.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. For the same mid-stride pose: that guess redraws the frame the camera should show, so a wrong hidden state is caught.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The fifth line. h sub t is the deterministic memory, the part of the hidden state that is computed, not drawn. f updates it from the last memory, the last hidden state and the last torques. h sub t minus 1 is the last memory. s hat sub t minus 1 is the last hidden state. a sub t minus 1 is the last torques. So the memory carries what happened forward step by step.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The memory carries the past forward: what happened stays available without a new frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. h sub t is the deterministic memory, the part of the hidden state that is computed, not drawn. f updates it from h sub t minus 1 , the last memory, s hat sub t minus 1 , the last hidden state, and a sub t minus 1 , the last torques. Nothing random enters here, so the memory carries what happened forward step by step. The memory feeds the random state at each step and rides inside the hidden state the actor and critic read.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. Two steps after the push-off: the memory still holds the push-off from two steps back, while the fresh random state says only where the body is now.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: So the five lines together are the world model: the frame pins down the hidden state, the transition guesses ahead without a frame, the reward line scores each arrival, the rebuild line teaches the hidden state what the camera shows, and the memory carries the past forward.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Training needs one score for the whole model, one that covers everything chance can do across the stored sequences. The score keeps the guess that works without the frame close to the guess that uses the frame with a KL divergence, how far one set of chances is from another.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. A world model is only useful if its guesses match what really happened, so its training needs one score to raise. This score rebuilds frames, predicts rewards, and keeps the guess that works without the frame close to the guess that uses the frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Equation 2. The model objective. A world model is only useful if its guesses match what really happened, so its training needs one score to raise.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The first line. J sub omega is the model objective, the one score training raises. E is the expected value over the stored sequences. The sum adds over every step t. The first log term scores q sub omega rebuilding the real frame o sub t from the hidden state s hat sub t. The second log term scores q sub omega predicting the real reward r sub t from the same hidden state. Beta times the K L gap penalizes the guess that works without the frame for drifting from p sub omega, the guess that uses the frame. So the objective rewards rebuilding frames and predicting rewards, and pulls the guess that works without the frame close to the guess that uses the frame.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. One score: rebuild frames, predict rewards, keep the guess that works without the frame close.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. J sub omega is the model objective. E is the expected value over the stored sequences, each sequence's score times its chance. The first term, log q sub omega of o sub t given s hat sub t , is the rebuild line's score for the real frame. The second term adds log q sub omega of r sub t given s hat sub t , the reward line's score for the real reward. The third term subtracts beta times the KL gap between p sub omega and q sub omega , penalizing the guess that works without the frame for drifting from the guess that uses the frame. beta weights the penalty: larger keeps the guess that works without the frame closer. J sub omega is that sum over every step t: the rebuild log plus the reward log minus beta times the KL gap between p sub omega and q sub omega .

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. When the walker stumbles in one stored sequence: at each step the hidden state must rebuild the frame and predict the reward.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: So one score trains the whole model: rebuild the frames, predict the rewards, and keep the guess that works without the frame close.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The rebuild term is not the only way to teach the hidden state. A contrastive objective instead drops the part that rebuilds the frame from the hidden state, the observation model, and trains a state model instead, a part that predicts the hidden state straight from the image. It learns by noise contrastive estimation: the state must pick the matching image out of a batch of wrong ones, so the states stay spread out instead of collapsing. On the 20 Control Suite tasks, the simulated robot tasks Dreamer was tested on, rebuilding solved the most, the contrastive version about half, and predicting rewards alone was not sufficient. Reach for it when rebuilding frames costs too much, or the frames carry little the task needs.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: 3.2 The actor picks torques and the critic scores them

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The reparameterization trick writes a random draw as the centre plus the width times a standard random number, so the critic's gradient can flow back into the actor.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The actor

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Picture the walker mid-stride in imagination: the actor is the policy network that picks the torques in imagined states.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: It gives one centre and one width per torque, and draws each torque from a Gaussian, a bell-shaped spread around the centre as wide as the width, as the centre plus the width times a standard random number, so gradients flow back through the model, then tanh, which squeezes any number into -1 to 1, squeezes each draw into the joints' allowed range.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Gradients flow back through the model into the actor, so imagined returns improve the torques without a real step.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The actor picks torques in imagined states and the critic scores those states, so imagination can train behaviour. The three lines are the actor's draw, the critic's score, and the trick that lets gradients flow back through the draw.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Equation 3. The actor and critic. The actor picks torques in imagined states and the critic scores those states, so imagination can train behaviour.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The first line. a sub j is the torque drawn at imagined step j. Pee sub thay-ta is the actor, the policy that picks the torques. s hat sub j is the imagined hidden state. So the actor draws a torque from its chances in each imagined state.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The actor draws torques in imagined states; the critic judges those states.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. a sub j is the torque drawn at imagined step j, and the tilde sign reads as drawn at random from. pee sub thay-ta of a sub j given s hat sub j is the actor, a tanh-transformed Gaussian over torques, with the small thay-ta under it the actor's weights; the bar reads as given. The small j under each symbol marks the imagined step, counted from the real moment t . a sub j is drawn from pee sub thay-ta of a sub j given s hat sub j . The actor draws with the reparameterization trick, the centre plus the width times a standard random number, so the gradient flows back into the actor, and tanh squeezes each draw into the joints' allowed range.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. With the walker balanced on one leg in imagination: the actor draws a torque for the ankle joint from its chances.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The second line. V sub fee is the critic's guess of the value of the imagined hidden state. Fee is the critic's weights. s hat sub j is the imagined hidden state. So the critic scores each imagined state by the return the walker expects from there.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The critic reads only the hidden state, no frame and no torque.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. V sub fee of s hat sub j is the critic's guess of the value of the imagined hidden state s hat sub j . The critic's guess is the return the walker expects from there, with the small fee under it the critic's weights. The critic reads only the hidden state, no frame and no torque.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. For the hidden state behind the balanced pose: the critic scores it, saying what return the walker expects from there.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The third line. a sub j is the torque at imagined step j. Mu sub thay-ta is its centre. Sigma sub thay-ta is its width. Epsilon is a standard random number, drawn from a bell centred at 0 with width 1. So the torque is the centre plus the width times a standard random number, squeezed by tanh into the joints' allowed range.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Intuition. The torque is a centre plus a width times a standard random number, squeezed into the joints' allowed range.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The mathematics. a sub j is the torque at imagined step j. mu sub thay-ta of s hat sub j is its centre, sigma sub thay-ta of s hat sub j its width, and epsilon is a standard random number, drawn from a Gaussian, a bell centred at 0 with width 1. I means each number is drawn on its own, with width 1. tanh squeezes each draw into the joints' allowed range, so no draw can exceed it.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Example. At the ankle joint: the centre says push a little forward, the width says how unsure the actor is, and the draw picks the actual torque.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: So the actor draws torques from a bell in each imagined state, the critic scores those states, and the reparameterization trick keeps the gradients flowing.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: 3.3 The target blends rewards with the critic's value

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Lambda, the mix weight, sets how much the longer sums count. The discount sets how much a reward one step later still counts. The target is what the critic learns to predict.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The lambda-return

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Picture the rollout ending before the payoff: the target blends the next reward with the critic's value and the next target, so it looks past the end.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The next reward comes first, then the next step's blend, counted a little less by the discount: one minus lambda times the critic's value, plus lambda times the next target.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: A short rollout ends before the payoff, so without this blend the actor would train only toward what pays inside the horizon.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. A short imagined rollout ends before the payoff arrives, so the critic needs a target that looks past the end of the rollout. This target blends the next reward with the critic's value and the next target.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: Equation 4. The lambda-return. A short imagined rollout ends before the payoff arrives, so the critic needs a target that looks past the end of the rollout.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The plot shows what the target leans on as the mix weight changes. At zero the target is one reward plus the critic's value; at one it is the longest reward sum plus the critic's value.

units.section: 3 The world model, the actor and the critic
units.spoken: The first line. V sub lambda of s hat sub j is this imagined state's target. r hat sub j plus 1 is the reward predicted one step ahead. Gamma is the discount, how much a reward one step later still counts. Lambda is the mix weight, how much the longer sums count. units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: Section five, Three short functions run one update

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: Three short functions run one update from a batch of real moments. The first imagines a rollout from each moment: the actor picks torques, the model steps the hidden state forward, and each step earns its predicted reward. The second walks back from the critic's value at the end, blending each reward with the value after it into targets. The third learns from those targets: the actor climbs toward higher targets and the critic moves toward them. The model's own training is left out. The update starts from hidden states pinned down by the guess that uses the frame.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: This code is the code name imagine: it imagines a rollout from a starting hidden state. At each imagined step the actor draws a torque, the transition guesses the next hidden state, and the reward line gives its mean. It gathers the states and the rewards into one list each and returns them stacked together.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: The rollout keeps one more state than the horizon counts, the start first. Each reward is the reward after the move taken from the state beside it, the predicted reward one step ahead. The torque draw and the hidden-state draw both keep their gradients: the guess that works without the frame steps the hidden state forward from the last state and the last torques, the actor draws the torque from its chances, and the reward line gives its mean. The start state is cut off from the gradients, so the rollout starts from a fixed hidden state. The per-step states and rewards are gathered into one list each.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: This code is the code name lambda return: it walks back from the critic's value at the end and blends each reward with the value after it into targets. The running total starts as the critic's value at the rollout's end, and reversing at the end puts each target beside its state.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: The running total starts as the critic's value at the rollout's end; each step pairs a reward with the value of the state after it; reversing at the end puts each target beside its state. The mix weight sets how much the longer sums count; the critic's value of each state comes in alongside the rewards.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: This code runs one update from a batch of real moments. It freezes the model and critic weights, imagines a rollout, and builds the targets. The actor's loss is minus the mean target, so minimizing it raises the targets. Then it unfreezes the weights and the critic moves toward the targets on every imagined state except the last.

units.section: 5 The three functions
units.spoken: The actor's update raises the expected sum of the targets over the imagined steps, turned into a loss to minimise by the minus sign. The critic's update shrinks the squared gap between the critic's guess and the target, on every imagined state except the last. The actor's loss averages one target per reward earned, while the paper's sum runs one term further, to the final imagined state. The final imagined state earns no reward after it, so it has no target of its own; its value is only the starting point for the walk back. The critic skips the final state because there its target equals its own guess, so the gap is zero. Freezing the model and critic weights still lets the actor's gradient flow through them, but writes nothing into them. The learned model here supplies the transition and reward lines. One updater changes the actor's weights, another the critic's.

units.section: 6 A hop that pays later
units.spoken: Section six, The critic lets short rollouts train toward late payoffs

units.section: 6 A hop that pays later
units.spoken: The walker is reactive: a good move pays almost at once, so it copes without a critic. A version without a critic and PlaNet succeed only on reactive tasks like it, so the tool uses Hopper Hop instead: a one-legged robot whose payoff comes many steps later. In this tool the Hopper first crouches, and only the hop after it pays. The critic has learned from past imagined rollouts that a crouched pose is worth a lot, because a hop usually follows it.

units.section: 6 A hop that pays later
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 5. Three imagined rollouts fan out from one real moment: crouch then hop, lean forward, and stand still. The horizon marks where imagination stops, and inside the horizon alone the critic adds what lies past it. The hop pays nothing inside the horizon, yet its bar stands tallest, because the critic knows the hop pays later.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Section seven, Training settings and results on 20 tasks

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: A longer horizon sees further ahead, but it leans on a model that grows less accurate the further it imagines. A higher mix weight trusts longer imagined sums of reward, while a lower one trusts the critic sooner. A larger action repeat, how many frames one chosen move is held for, makes each imagined step cover more real time.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: The settings that shape the behaviour:

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Imagination horizon H : 15 steps.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Lambda-return weight lambda : 0.95.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Discount gamma : 0.99.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: KL weight beta : 1, with 3 free nats (a nat is the unit the KL term is measured in; the KL term stops pushing once it is already small).

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Training steps per collected episode: 100.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Batch: 50 sequences of length 50; a larger batch steadies each update, a smaller one runs cheaper.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Optimizer and learning rates: Adam, an optimizer that gives each weight its own step size, with 6e-4 for the model and 8e-5 each for the actor and the critic.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Gradient norm clip: 100 (the norm is the gradient's length; longer gradients are scaled down to this length); a higher clip lets longer gradients through, a lower one steadies training.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Random episodes to start: 5; more seed episodes give a wider start, fewer start narrower.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Action repeat: 2.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Exploration noise: Normal(0, 0.3), a bell-shaped draw centred at 0 with width 0.3; more noise tries wilder moves, less noise sticks to what works.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Images: 64 by 64.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Dreamer needed no slow-moving copy of the critic to build its targets and no extra reward for staying undecided. For tasks that can end early, the model also predicts whether the episode continues.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: A higher learning rate takes bigger steps and can overshoot; a lower one takes smaller, steadier steps. Dreamer uses a separate learning rate for the model, the actor and the critic.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Each training run used one Nvidia V100 GPU and 10 CPU cores and took about 3 hours per million real steps. Imagining stays cheap because it runs in the compact latent space: each hidden state pairs a 200-number deterministic memory with a 30-number random state. Only the reward function is three layers of 300 units; the transition is the recurrent state space model, and frame rebuilding is a transposed convolutional decoder. The authors released the code under the name Dreamer.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: 7.1 Walking and balancing from pixels on DeepMind Control

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Dreamer trained on 20 DeepMind Control Suite tasks from 64 by 64 camera images, with the same settings for every task: action repeat 2, episodes of 1,000 steps, actions of 1 to 12 torques, rewards from 0 to 1. The tasks include the walker, the hopper, the acrobot, a two-link arm that must swing up, the quadruped, a four-legged robot that must walk, and cup catch, a ball on a string to catch in a cup. Each seed is one full training run from a different random start, and the results average 5 seeds.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: After 5 million real steps Dreamer averaged a score of 823 across the 20 tasks. The model-based agent PlaNet averaged 332 at the same 5 million steps. D4PG is a model-free method: it learns values straight from real steps, with no model of the world. It is also a distributed agent: many copies play in parallel and feed one learner. D4PG averaged 786 after 100 million steps. At a horizon of 20, Dreamer beat the alternatives on 16 of 20 tasks and tied on 4.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Let's take a look at figure 8. Three bars compare the mean score across the 20 tasks against the real steps each agent needed. Dreamer reaches 823 after 5 million real steps. PlaNet reaches 332 after the same 5 million steps. D4PG reaches 786, but only after 100 million steps. So Dreamer tops both rivals on a twentieth of the real steps D4PG needed.

units.section: 7 The settings that matter
units.spoken: Dreamer tops both rivals on a twentieth of the real steps D4PG needed.

units.section: 8 How far dreaming goes
units.spoken: Section eight, Control from pixels with few real steps

units.section: 8 How far dreaming goes
units.spoken: Dreamer fits when the actions are amounts, the observations are images, and real steps are scarce.

units.section: 8 How far dreaming goes
units.spoken: Dreamer also runs on discrete actions, one move from a list instead of an amount per joint: it was tried on Atari games, the arcade games of the 1980s played from the screen alone, and DeepMind Lab levels, first-person 3D maze tasks, with a horizon of 10 and a KL weight of 0.1.

units.section: 8 How far dreaming goes
units.spoken: Against MuZero, which searches through possible moves at decision time, Dreamer acts without searching, so acting is cheap and continuous actions work directly.

units.section: 8 How far dreaming goes
units.spoken: Against D4PG, a model-free agent that learns from stored steps: it fits when real steps are cheap enough for many copies to play in parallel, while Dreamer fits when they are scarce; the cost is a model to tune.

sections.section: 9 When the model is wrong and the horizon runs short

units.section: 9 When the model is wrong and the horizon runs short
units.spoken: Section nine, When the model is wrong and the horizon runs short

units.section: 9 When the model is wrong and the horizon runs short
units.spoken: Model exploitation: the actor finds actions where the model is wrong, so imagined returns climb while real ones do not, as when a move that scores inside imagination scores nothing for real. Keeping the model training on new real episodes closes the blind spots the actor steers into, and a short horizon gives the model less room to be wrong.

units.section: 9 When the model is wrong and the horizon runs short
units.spoken: A reward alone is too sparse to shape the hidden state, so the hidden state misses what the task needs and imagined rollouts go wrong.
